 Global minimum tax: how it works, and the deadlines putting pressure on large groups
 Aurel Dragan 
 20/10/2026 | 12:18 
 Twitter 
 Facebook 
 Linkedin 
 The implementation of the OECD’s Pillar 2 has moved from the legislative phase to that of effective compliance, and multinational and domestic groups with consolidated revenues exceeding €750 million have specific obligations regarding the calculation, reporting and declaration of the additional tax. 
 An opinion by: Răzvan Ungureanu, Partner, Head of International Tax Advisory Services, EY Romania 
 In Romania, the mechanism is regulated by Law No. 431/2023, which transposes the European Directive on the global minimum tax and introduces the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax – QDMTT) and applies to both multinational groups (such as OMV, Renault and Ford) and large Romanian groups (such as Banca Transilvania, Dedeman and Altex). 
 Although public attention has often focused on the 15 per cent minimum threshold, the real challenge for companies is the new compliance framework. QDMTT is just one component of this system, alongside the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) and the Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR); it is the mechanism through which Romania reserves the right to collect the tax difference relating to locally generated profits up to the minimum tax rate of 15%.
 For many groups, the impact will not be determined solely by the level of the additional tax, but by their ability to collect data, carry out complex calculations and manage a new tax reporting process on a global scale.  A key, yet often underestimated, factor is that a full breakdown of the QDMTT calculation is not required if at least one of the three tests under the CbCR Safe Harbour transitional regime is met: the de minimis test, the simplified ETR test and the routine profits test. The data used is drawn from the qualified Country-by-Country (CbCR) report and from the financial statements prepared in accordance with the applicable accounting standard at group level, which may differ from the standard used for calculations under local rules.
 The CbCR Safe Harbour transitional period is time-limited, applying to the financial years 2024–2027, following the latest amendments. For financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026, the simplified ETR test uses a threshold of 17%. 
 Treatment of specific items affecting the ETR 
 In practice, the adjustment of the effective tax rate (ETR) is directly influenced by the treatment of certain local tax incentives. For example, current and deferred corporation tax, as recognised in the explanatory notes to statutory or IFRS financial statements, is relevant for determining the taxes covered in the QDMTT calculation. Incentives such as the tax credit for sponsorship, the exemption for reinvested profits, the equity bonus and additional deductions for research and development activities may have different effects on the ETR. The treatment of each incentive must be analysed in light of its compliance with the GloBE rules and the available documentation. 
 Experience from the first reporting cycle (mentioned above) shows that preparing the dossier and validating the data should not be left until the very end of the compliance period, and reporting can no longer be treated as a task to be left until the last minute before the deadline.
 For the 2024 financial year, in the case of groups with a calendar year as their financial year for which this was the transition year, the 18-month deadline resulted in a deadline of 30 June 2026. For the 2025 financial year, the general deadline is no later than 15 months from the last day of the reporting financial year, i.e. 31 March 2027 for groups with a calendar year. The same 15-month deadline applies to the declaration and payment of supplementary tax and national supplementary tax, in accordance with Article 48 of Law No. 431/2023. For financial years that do not align with the calendar year, the exact date is calculated individually from the last day of the financial year.
 The shorter reporting window makes it necessary to bring forward key activities before the end of the following financial year. Consequently, our recommendation for companies whose financial year coincides with the calendar year is that preparations for reporting should begin as early as 2026, rather than in the first quarter of 2027. This is all the more important given that an estimate of potential liabilities is also required for the financial statements for that year, which have a much earlier submission deadline than the deadlines for submitting the global minimum tax returns.
 2027 reporting checklist 
 1. Confirmation of the scope and responsibilities 
 The inventory of constituent entities, permanent establishments, the control structure and the entity that will submit the return must be finalised before the end of the year. If the payment of the supplementary national tax is to be made by a single designated entity in Romania, the option must be exercised within the statutory six-month period from the last day of the reporting financial year by submitting the relevant notification.
 2. Data dictionary and accounting sources 
 The sources for the accounting profit, current and deferred taxes, GloBE adjustments, payroll costs and eligible tangible fixed assets must be established in advance. Each field should have a responsible party, source, currency, conversion rule and reconciliation evidence.
 3. Reconciliation between local, consolidated and CbCR 
 Statutory data, consolidation packages and the qualified CbCR report must be compared prior to submission. Differences in accounting standards, intra-group eliminations and consolidation adjustments must be documented, as they may alter the outcome of the Safe Harbour tests and the ETR calculation.
 4. Safe Harbour testing before the end of the year 
 For each jurisdiction, the three applicable tests must be carried out and supporting documentation retained. It is also important to verify continued eligibility, as failure to apply the regime in a given year may prevent its subsequent use for that jurisdiction, in accordance with Article 36(12).
 5. Inventory of GloBE options 
 The group must decide on and document its annual or five-year options, including those relating to the exclusion of profit from activities with economic substance, qualifying losses or special treatments. The disclosure statement must include a record of the options exercised.
 6. Preliminary calculation and payment scenarios 
 A calculation based on interim data enables the identification of jurisdictions with an ETR below 15 per cent, significant adjustments and any potential payment obligations. The result must be updated after the year-end, not built from scratch.
 7. Audit trail and internal approval 
 The company should prepare a comprehensive audit trail: data sources, reconciliations, assumptions, technical decisions, calculation versions and approvals. It is also useful to carry out a final check of the ANAF forms and instructions in force at the time of submission.
 For the 2027 reporting, early preparation will make all the difference: a confirmed scope, reconciled data, clear responsibilities and a preliminary calculation before the end of the year. The statutory deadline remains important, but the real challenge is for the group to reach the deadline with its technical positions already documented and a complete audit trail in place. Pillar II, at least in the light of the first mandatory filings due in the middle of this year, is proving to be not merely a calculation exercise, but a true test of the maturity of the tax function.
